title: The Guru Granth Sahib and Ahimsa
bigQuestion: How do Sikhs and Jains turn a central conviction, one God for Sikhs and non-harm for Jains, into daily practice that anyone can see?

story.title: The Kitchen With No Head of the Table
story.kicker: In a gurdwara kitchen northwest of Chicago, a retired engineer and a first-year student peel the same pile of onions, and no one asks who is more important.
paragraphs: It is a Sunday morning in Palatine, Illinois. Inside a large white building topped with domes, a kitchen is already loud. Steam rises from pots of lentils big enough to bathe in. A retired engineer in a blue turban stirs one pot with a paddle. Beside him a first-year college student, her head covered with a scarf, peels onions and blinks back tears. Neither of them was assigned this job. They came early because the work needed doing.

Down the hall, in a wide room with a carpeted floor, people are taking their places for the meal. There are no chairs. Everyone sits on the floor in long rows, shoulder to shoulder: a doctor next to a bus driver, a grandmother next to a teenager in a hoodie, a visitor who has never been inside a gurdwara next to a man who has come every week for forty years. Volunteers walk the rows with buckets and ladles, serving flatbread, lentils, vegetables and rice pudding to anyone who holds out a plate.

This meal is called the *langar*, and it has been served this way for about five hundred years. Sikh tradition traces it to Guru Nanak, who taught that a person's worth does not depend on caste, wealth, gender or religion. Sitting in a row on the floor to eat the same food makes that teaching visible. In Sikh understanding, you cannot claim to be above the person beside you while sharing a plate of lentils on the same carpet.

The Golden Temple in Amritsar, India, serves this meal to tens of thousands of people every day, and no one is charged and no one is turned away. Smaller gurdwaras across the Chicago area do the same on a smaller scale. The food is plain and vegetarian so that people of every faith and diet can eat it. In this unit, that kitchen is a good place to begin, because it shows a belief becoming a practice that anyone can watch, join or study.

Later the chapter moves to a very different community, the Jains of India, whose central conviction is *ahimsa*, non-harm toward every living thing. Jains also turn a belief into daily choices, about what to eat, what to wear, and even how to walk. Two traditions, two convictions, and in each case a practice you could recognize from across a room.
story.think: The langar puts a teaching about equality into a seating arrangement. What is one other practice, from any tradition or none, where an idea about people is built into how a room or a meal is set up?

sections.title: Guru Nanak and the Ten Gurus

lessons.title: Nanak's Journey and Message
lessons.mainIdea: Sikh tradition begins with Guru Nanak, who taught devotion to one God and rejected divisions between people.
reading: Sikh tradition tells that Nanak was born in 1469 in the village of Talwandi in the Punjab, a region that today lies on both sides of the India–Pakistan border. His family was Hindu, and his neighbors included many Muslims. According to the traditional accounts called the *janamsakhis*, at about age thirty Nanak went to bathe in a river and disappeared for three days. When he returned, tradition says, his first words were that there is no Hindu and no Muslim. Sikhs understand this to mean that God is not the property of any one group and that the labels people fight over do not matter to God.

After that experience Nanak spent roughly two decades traveling. Sikh sources describe journeys east to Bengal, south toward Sri Lanka, north into the Himalayas and west to Mecca and Baghdad. On these trips, tradition says, he sang his teachings and debated with religious leaders. A Muslim musician named Mardana traveled with him and played a stringed instrument called the rabab while Nanak sang. This pairing of a Hindu-born teacher and a Muslim companion has remained an important image for Sikhs.

Around 1520 Nanak settled at Kartarpur, on the banks of the Ravi River, and founded a community. Followers farmed, worked and worshiped together, and they came to be called *Sikhs*, a Punjabi word meaning learners or disciples. Nanak is called *Guru*, which in Sikh usage means the teacher who carries God's word to people. Sikhs believe that the Guru's role is not to be worshiped but to point the learner toward the one God.

Scholars note that Nanak lived at a time when devotional movements were flourishing in North India. Poets such as Kabir taught love of God beyond caste and ritual, and Sufi Muslim teachers sang of God in the local languages. Sikhs hold that Nanak's message was a direct revelation, not a blend of other faiths, and the academic study of religion describes both the setting and the community's own understanding without choosing between them.

words.d: a learner or disciple; a follower of the teachings of Guru Nanak and the Gurus who came after him
in Sikh usage, the teacher who carries God's word to people; the title of Nanak and his nine successors
traditional stories of Guru Nanak's life, written down in the generations after him
the region of the Indus River's five tributaries, now split between India and Pakistan; the homeland of Sikhism

look.title: Reading a Founding Story
look.text: The janamsakhis say that when Nanak emerged from the river after three days, he declared that there is no Hindu and no Muslim. Some readers take this as a statement that both labels are false. Sikh teachers usually read it differently: that God does not judge people by the religion they were born into, and that people of both groups had drifted from true devotion.
look.prompt: Using the author-audience-purpose toolkit from Unit 13, explain why the community's own reading matters when you study a founding story, and how you would report both readings without choosing one.

check.q: What does the word Sikh mean in Punjabi?
check.why: Sikh means learner or disciple, which fits the tradition's picture of a person who learns from the Guru.

check.q: Who was Mardana in Sikh tradition?
choices: A Muslim musician who traveled with Nanak
A Hindu king who opposed Nanak
check.why: Mardana, a Muslim musician, played the rabab while Nanak sang, and Sikhs treasure this image of companionship across religious lines.

check.q: Where did Guru Nanak settle and found a community around 1520?
check.why: Nanak founded the community at Kartarpur on the Ravi River. Amritsar was founded later by the fourth Guru.

lessons.title: Ten Gurus, One Light
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs believe the same divine light passed through ten human Gurus, from Nanak in 1469 to Gobind Singh, who died in 1708.
reading: Before his death in 1539, Guru Nanak chose a follower named Lehna as his successor and renamed him Angad, a word Sikhs connect to the idea of a limb of one's own body. Sikhs believe that the Guruship then passed from person to person, ten Gurus in all, and that each carried the same light. A common Sikh image is one candle lighting the next: the flame is the same even though the candle changes. For this reason Sikhs speak of the Gurus with the same reverence and often refer to them together as a single Guru.

Several Gurus shaped the community's institutions. The third Guru, Amar Das, made the langar meal a fixed practice and asked visitors to eat in it before meeting him. The fourth, Ram Das, founded the city of Amritsar. The fifth, Arjan, built the Harmandir Sahib, known in English as the Golden Temple, at the center of a pool in Amritsar and compiled the community's scripture in 1604. In 1606 Guru Arjan died in the custody of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, and Sikhs remember him as the first Sikh martyr.

After Arjan's death, the sixth Guru, Hargobind, began to wear two swords, which Sikhs interpret as *miri* and *piri*, worldly authority and spiritual authority. The ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi in 1675 on the orders of the emperor Aurangzeb. Sikh tradition holds that he died defending the right of Hindus in Kashmir to practice their religion. Sikhs point to this as an example of standing up for the freedom of others.

The tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, was Tegh Bahadur's son and became Guru at age nine. In 1699 he founded the *Khalsa*, a community of initiated Sikhs, which a later lesson describes. Before he died in 1708, Sikh tradition says he declared that there would be no more human Gurus and that the scripture itself would serve as Guru from then on. Historians also note that all four of Gobind Singh's sons died in the conflicts of his lifetime, a loss Sikhs remember in prayer.

words.d: the city in the Punjab founded by the fourth Guru, Ram Das, and home to the Harmandir Sahib
the central Sikh shrine in Amritsar, often called the Golden Temple in English
worldly and spiritual authority, symbolized by the two swords worn by the sixth Guru, Hargobind
a person who dies rather than give up a belief; Sikhs count Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur among their martyrs

look.title: The Ten Gurus in Order
look.cite: Standard dates given in Sikh histories; the seventh and eighth Gurus, Har Rai and Har Krishan, served between 1644 and 1664
look.prompt: Two of the Gurus listed took office in the year another Guru died in custody or was executed. Which years are they, and what does that tell you about the pressures on the community in the 1600s?

check.q: How do Sikhs describe the relationship among the ten Gurus?
choices: Ten rival teachers with different messages
One light passing from candle to candle
check.why: Sikhs use the image of one flame lighting a series of candles: the Guruship was the same light in ten human beings.

check.q: Which Guru compiled the Sikh scripture in 1604 and built the Harmandir Sahib?
check.why: The fifth Guru, Arjan, compiled the scripture and built the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar; he died in Mughal custody in 1606.

check.q: Why do Sikhs remember the death of Guru Tegh Bahadur in 1675?
choices: He died in battle leading an army
He was executed after defending the religious freedom of Hindus in Kashmir
He founded Amritsar and died there
He was the last Guru and ended the line
check.why: Sikh tradition holds that Tegh Bahadur was executed in Delhi for standing up for Kashmiri Hindus' right to practice their faith.

lessons.title: The Scripture That Is the Guru
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as their living Guru, a book of hymns that is honored, sung and consulted rather than simply read.
reading: Walk into any gurdwara and you will see the same thing at the front of the main hall: a large book resting on cushions under a canopy, with an attendant waving a whisk over it. That book is the *Guru Granth Sahib*, and for Sikhs it is not a symbol of the Guru but the Guru itself. Sikhs believe that in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh ended the line of human Gurus and gave that role to the scripture. People bow before it, sit lower than it, and carry it to a bed each night in a ceremony of rest.

The standard printed edition has 1,430 pages, and every copy uses the same page layout so that a hymn is on the same page everywhere in the world. The text is written in *Gurmukhi*, a script the second Guru is credited with shaping, though the languages inside include Punjabi, Hindi, Persian and others. Almost the whole book is poetry set to music. It is organized by *raga*, the musical modes of Indian tradition, rather than by topic, because it was meant to be sung.

The Guru Granth Sahib contains the hymns of six of the Sikh Gurus. It also includes the compositions of Hindu and Muslim poets, such as Kabir, Namdev and the Sufi teacher Farid. Sikhs call these poets the *bhagats*. Sikhs see this as a sign that truth is not confined to one community. The book opens with the *Mul Mantar*, a short statement of who God is. It names God as one, true, creator, without fear or enmity, beyond time, not born, self-existent, and known by the Guru's grace.

Because the scripture is the Guru, Sikhs do not have priests in the sense of a separate class with special authority over the text. Any Sikh, man or woman, who can read Gurmukhi may lead a service. A reader called a *granthi* cares for the book and reads from it, and a continuous reading of the whole text from start to finish, called an Akhand Path, takes about forty-eight hours and marks important occasions. At the end of a service, the book is opened at random and the hymn on that page is read as the day's guidance.

words.d: the Sikh scripture, a collection of hymns that Sikhs honor as their living and final Guru
the script in which the Guru Granth Sahib is written; the name means from the mouth of the Guru
a musical mode of Indian tradition; the Sikh scripture is arranged by raga because its hymns are meant to be sung
Hindu and Muslim devotional poets, such as Kabir and Farid, whose hymns are included in the Guru Granth Sahib
the reader who cares for and reads from the Guru Granth Sahib in a gurdwara; not a priest with separate authority

look.title: The Opening Words
look.text: The scripture opens by declaring that there is one God, whose name is truth, who is the creator, who is without fear and without hatred, who is beyond time, who is not born and does not die, who exists by God's own being, and who is known through the Guru's grace. The passage then says that this One was true in the beginning, is true now, and will be true always.
look.cite: Guru Granth Sahib, opening lines (the Mul Mantar and the first verse of the Japji of Guru Nanak), page 1; paraphrased from Macauliffe's 1909 translation
look.prompt: List the qualities of God named in this opening. Which of them would Muslims and Jews also affirm from their own texts, and which language is distinctly Sikh?

check.q: Why do Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib?
choices: Because it was written by God's own hand
Because it is the oldest book in India
Because they believe it holds the office of Guru after the ten human Gurus
Because Guru Nanak asked to be worshiped
check.why: Sikhs believe Guru Gobind Singh gave the Guruship to the scripture in 1708, so they honor it as the Guru, not as an idol.

check.q: How is the Guru Granth Sahib organized?
choices: By topic, from creation to the end of time
By the date each hymn was written
By the age of each Guru
check.why: Almost the whole book is poetry meant to be sung, so it is arranged by raga rather than by subject or date.

check.q: Who are the bhagats whose hymns appear in the Sikh scripture?
choices: Hindu and Muslim devotional poets such as Kabir and Farid
The five Sikhs who first joined the Khalsa
check.why: The bhagats are non-Sikh poets whose compositions were included; Sikhs read this as a sign that truth is not owned by one community.

lessons.title: Ik Onkar and the Three Duties
lessons.mainIdea: Sikh teaching centers on remembering the one God while working honestly and sharing with others.
reading: The first symbol in the Guru Granth Sahib, and the one you will see on Sikh flags and doorways, is *Ik Onkar*. It combines the numeral one with a letter and is usually translated as There is one God, or One Reality is. For Sikhs it states the heart of the faith: God is one, without form, present everywhere, the same for every people. Sikhs use many names for God, including Waheguru, Wonderful Teacher, but hold that no image can represent God and that no place or people has an exclusive claim.

According to the Gurus, the main obstacle between a person and God is *haumai*, a Punjabi word for self-centeredness, the habit of putting I and mine at the center of everything. The remedy Sikhs practice is *naam simran*, remembering God's name. This can mean repeating a name of God quietly, singing the hymns, or holding God in mind during ordinary work. Sikhs believe that a life shaped by this remembrance slowly loosens the grip of ego and brings a person into harmony with God's will, called *hukam*.

Sikhs commonly summarize the Gurus' teaching in three duties, often given in Punjabi: *naam japna*, remembering God; *kirat karni*, earning an honest living; and *vand chakna*, sharing what you earn with those in need. Notice that two of the three are about ordinary economic life. Sikh tradition praises the householder who works and raises a family over the ascetic who withdraws from the world. A story told about Guru Nanak has him choosing a poor carpenter's plain bread over a rich man's feast because the carpenter's bread was earned honestly.

Sikhs, like Hindus and Buddhists, speak of karma and rebirth, and they believe the human birth is a rare chance to unite with God. But the Sikh account of liberation is centered on grace. Sikhs hold that a person cannot earn union with God by effort alone; the Guru's grace opens the way. Compare this with the Christian language of grace, or with the Jain emphasis on individual effort in a later lesson. That comparison is one of the useful exercises of this unit.

words.d: the opening symbol of the Sikh scripture, usually translated There is one God; the central Sikh statement of belief
self-centeredness or ego, which Sikh teaching names as the main barrier between a person and God
remembering God's name through repetition, singing or mindful attention during daily life
God's will or order; Sikhs seek to live in harmony with it
sharing one's earnings with those in need; one of the three duties Sikhs draw from the Gurus

look.title: A Carpenter's Bread
look.text: A traditional story tells that Guru Nanak, visiting a town, stayed with a poor carpenter named Lalo and ate his plain bread instead of attending the feast of a wealthy official named Malik Bhago. When the official demanded an explanation, the story says Nanak squeezed both breads: milk flowed from the carpenter's and blood from the official's, because one was earned honestly and the other by squeezing the poor.
look.prompt: This story is teaching kirat karni, honest work. What is the story claiming about wealth, and how would you describe its message without asserting that the miracle happened?

check.q: What does Ik Onkar mean?
check.why: Ik Onkar, the opening of the Sikh scripture, is usually translated There is one God.

check.q: What does Sikh teaching name as the main obstacle between a person and God?
choices: Being born in the wrong caste
check.why: Haumai, ego or self-centeredness, is the barrier the Gurus name; the remedy is naam simran, remembering God.

check.q: Which of these is one of the three duties Sikhs draw from the Gurus?
check.why: Kirat karni, honest work, joins naam japna and vand chakna as the three duties; Sikhism praises the working householder.

lessons.title: Seva and the Langar
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs express the equality of all people through seva, selfless service, most visibly in the free langar meal.
reading: Return to the kitchen from the opening story. The people cooking, cleaning and serving there are performing *seva*, selfless service done without expecting reward. Sikhs regard seva as a form of worship, not a chore attached to it. Sweeping the floor of a gurdwara, polishing the shoes of visitors, or washing the enormous pots after the meal are all seva. Many Sikhs describe the experience as a way of wearing down haumai, the ego, by putting oneself at the service of others.

The *langar* is the free community kitchen and the meal it serves. Sikh tradition credits Guru Nanak with beginning it and the third Guru, Amar Das, with making it a firm rule. He is said to have required that everyone, including the Mughal emperor Akbar when he visited, sit in the rows and eat before meeting him. The rows themselves, called *pangat*, are the point. In sixteenth-century India, people of different castes did not eat together, and a high-caste person could be considered polluted by sharing food with a low-caste one. The langar deliberately broke that rule.

The Gurus also addressed the position of women. Guru Nanak wrote a hymn asking why anyone should call woman inferior when kings are born of women. Sikh teaching holds that women and men are equally able to read the scripture, lead worship, and receive initiation into the Khalsa. Historians point out that practice in Sikh communities has not always matched this ideal, as in every tradition, and Sikh reformers today often quote these hymns when calling for change.

The scale of the langar can be startling. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar serves free meals to tens of thousands of people each day, prepared largely by volunteers. During disasters, Sikh organizations have set up mobile langars for flood victims and, in 2020, for people affected by the pandemic in cities around the world, including Chicago. Studying the langar is a way to see how a teaching about God's view of people becomes a rule about seating, a menu, and a schedule of volunteers.

words.d: selfless service done without expecting reward; Sikhs regard it as a form of worship
the free community kitchen at a gurdwara and the vegetarian meal it serves to everyone
the rows in which people sit on the floor to eat the langar, symbolizing the equality of everyone present
the hereditary social ranking of South Asia, which the Sikh Gurus rejected as a measure of a person's worth

look.title: Two Answers to One Question
look.text: Ask two traditions how a community should feed the hungry. A Sikh gurdwara answers with the langar: a free vegetarian meal for anyone, eaten together on the floor, prepared by volunteers as worship. Islam answers in part with zakat, a required share of wealth given each year to the poor, which the giver may distribute through a mosque or charity. Both feed people; the design differs.
look.prompt: Compare the two: who gives, who receives, whether giver and receiver meet, and what each practice is meant to teach the giver. Describe the difference without ranking the two.

check.q: Why do Sikhs regard washing pots after the langar as worship?
choices: It is seva, selfless service that wears down the ego
The Gurus required every Sikh to be a cook
Pots are sacred objects in Sikh teaching
It replaces the need to read the scripture
check.why: Seva, service done without reward, is itself a form of worship in Sikh understanding; washing pots or sweeping counts.

check.q: What rule of sixteenth-century Indian society did the langar deliberately break?
choices: The rule that meals must be eaten at night
The rule that people of different castes should not eat together
The rule that only kings could host feasts
The rule that food must be blessed by a priest
check.why: Sitting in pangat, mixed rows on the floor, rejected the caste rule against sharing food across social ranks.

check.q: What did Guru Nanak's hymn about women argue?
choices: That women should not enter the gurdwara
That women should serve the langar but not lead worship
That women should be honored as the ones from whom kings are born
That women should live apart from men
check.why: The hymn asks why anyone should call woman inferior when kings are born of women; Sikh teaching affirms equal standing in worship.

lessons.title: The Khalsa and the Five Ks
lessons.mainIdea: In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, whose initiated members wear five visible signs of their commitment.
reading: Sikh tradition tells that on the spring festival of Vaisakhi in 1699, at Anandpur in the Punjab hills, Guru Gobind Singh stood before a large gathering with a drawn sword and asked who was willing to give his head for the faith. One man stepped forward and was led into a tent. The Guru returned alone with a bloodied sword and asked again. Four more came forward in turn. Then, the story says, all five walked out of the tent alive and dressed in new robes. Sikhs call them the *Panj Piare*, the Five Beloved Ones. They came from different castes and different parts of India.

The Guru then prepared *amrit*, sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, gave it to the five, and then asked them to give it to him. Sikhs point to this moment as the founding of the *Khalsa*, a word meaning pure or belonging directly to God. Members took a new name: men became Singh, lion, and women became Kaur, princess. Because these names replaced caste surnames, they made it harder to tell a person's social rank, which Sikhs understand as part of the point. Today many Sikhs carry these names whether or not they have been initiated.

Initiated Sikhs, called *Amritdhari*, maintain five articles of faith whose Punjabi names all begin with K: *kesh*, uncut hair, usually kept under a turban by men and by some women; *kangha*, a small wooden comb that keeps the hair neat; *kara*, a steel bracelet worn on the wrist; *kachera*, cotton undershorts; and *kirpan*, a small sword. Sikhs explain them in various ways. The kara, for instance, is often described as a reminder of God's oneness and of the wearer's duty to act rightly with the hand that wears it. The kirpan represents the duty to defend the weak.

Not every Sikh is initiated, and Sikhs disagree among themselves about how strictly the five Ks must be kept. A student in a Chicago classroom might wear a turban and a kara, only a kara, or no visible sign at all, and still identify as Sikh. In the United States the kirpan has raised questions in schools and airports, and courts and school districts have often allowed small, secured kirpans as an exercise of religious freedom. Studying the five Ks is a case of the general question this course asks: how visible signs carry a community's memory and commitments.

words.d: the community of initiated Sikhs founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699; the word means pure or belonging to God
the Five Beloved Ones, the first five Sikhs to offer their lives and be initiated at Anandpur in 1699
sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, given to Sikhs at initiation into the Khalsa
the small sword carried by initiated Sikhs as a sign of the duty to defend the weak; one of the five Ks
uncut hair, kept as a sign of acceptance of God's creation; one of the five Ks, usually covered by a turban

look.title: Five Signs, Read From Outside and Inside
look.text: A person who knows nothing about Sikhs sees a steel bracelet, a turban and a small sword and may guess they are jewelry, a fashion and a weapon. An initiated Sikh sees a reminder of God's oneness, a covering for hair kept as God gave it, and a pledge to protect the vulnerable. The objects are the same; the meanings are not.
look.prompt: Pick one of the five Ks and write two short descriptions: one an outsider might give from appearance alone, and one a Sikh would give. What does the difference teach about studying religious dress in general?

check.q: What happened at Anandpur on Vaisakhi in 1699, according to Sikh tradition?
choices: The Guru Granth Sahib was completed
Guru Nanak returned from the river
Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa with the Panj Piare
check.why: Sikh tradition places the founding of the Khalsa at Anandpur in 1699, when five volunteers became the Panj Piare.

check.q: Why did the names Singh and Kaur matter socially?
choices: They replaced caste surnames, hiding a person's social rank
They showed which village a person came from
They were given only to nobles
They marked a person as a granthi
check.why: Singh and Kaur replaced family names that revealed caste, which fit the Gurus' rejection of caste ranking.

check.q: Which of the five Ks is a steel bracelet?
check.why: The kara is the steel bracelet; kesh is uncut hair, kangha the comb, and kachera the cotton undershorts.

sections.title: The Gurdwara and Sikhs in America

lessons.title: Inside a Gurdwara
lessons.mainIdea: A gurdwara is any place where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed, and its layout teaches openness and equality.
reading: The Sikh house of worship is a *gurdwara*, a word meaning door of the Guru. Any building where the Guru Granth Sahib is properly installed can be one, from a room in a house to the Harmandir Sahib. Most gurdwaras fly a tall flag called the *Nishan Sahib*, usually saffron or blue, marked with the *khanda*, a symbol of a double-edged sword, a circle and two curved swords. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar famously has four doors, one on each side, which Sikhs describe as a welcome to people from every direction and every background.

Visitors of any faith may enter a gurdwara. The protocol is the same for everyone: remove your shoes, cover your head, and do not bring tobacco or alcohol. In the main hall, called the *diwan* hall, worshipers walk to the front, bow to the Guru Granth Sahib, often leave an offering, and sit on the carpeted floor. Men and women usually sit on opposite sides, though this is custom rather than scripture. There are no statues or images of God, in keeping with the Sikh belief that God has no form.

The heart of a Sikh service is *kirtan*, the singing of hymns from the scripture, usually to harmonium and tabla drums. A speaker may explain a hymn, and the service closes with a standing prayer called the Ardas, which recalls the Gurus and the martyrs and asks for the good of all humanity. Then the book is opened at random and a hymn is read aloud as guidance. Everyone receives *karah prasad*, a warm sweet made of flour, clarified butter and sugar, handed out from a single bowl so that no one receives anything different from anyone else.

The gurdwara is also a school, a community center and a kitchen. Children learn Punjabi and Gurmukhi there on weekends. Weddings, called Anand Karaj, take place in front of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the couple walks around the scripture four times while a hymn is sung. Sikh calendars mark the birthdays of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, Vaisakhi in April, and the martyrdom days of Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur, all observed with kirtan and langar.

words.d: a Sikh house of worship, literally the door of the Guru; any place where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed
the tall saffron or blue flag flown outside a gurdwara, bearing the khanda symbol
the singing of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib, the central act of Sikh worship
a warm sweet made of flour, clarified butter and sugar given to everyone at the end of a Sikh service
the Sikh wedding ceremony, held before the Guru Granth Sahib

look.title: A Field Trip Checklist
look.text: Your class is visiting a gurdwara in the Chicago suburbs. A classmate asks: Do I have to bow? Can I take pictures? What if I do not eat what they serve? Why is the flag orange? Where do I sit? Another classmate is worried about wearing a head covering because of her own religion.
look.prompt: Using the lesson, write the guidance you would give each classmate, and explain which parts are rules of respect for the host community and which parts are optional for a visitor who is studying, not practicing.

check.q: What makes a building a gurdwara?
choices: The Guru Granth Sahib properly installed inside
A statue of Guru Nanak at the entrance
check.why: A gurdwara is the door of the Guru; the presence of the installed scripture, not the architecture, makes the place.

check.q: Why is karah prasad served from a single bowl to everyone?
choices: To save time during large services
Because the recipe requires one pot
So that no one receives anything different from anyone else
Because only the granthi may touch the bowl
check.why: Sharing one sweet from one bowl expresses the equality of everyone present, as the langar does.

check.q: Which of these is the central act of a Sikh service?
choices: Kirtan, the singing of hymns from the scripture

lessons.title: Sikhs in America and Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs have lived in the United States for over a century, and the Chicago area has a large and active Sikh community.
reading: Sikhism is a global tradition of roughly 25 to 30 million people, according to common estimates, which makes it one of the larger religions in the world though far smaller than Hinduism or Islam. Most Sikhs live in the Indian state of Punjab. Large communities also live in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, Malaysia and East Africa. Estimates of the Sikh population in the United States usually fall between 500,000 and 700,000, with the largest concentrations in California, New York and New Jersey.

The first Sikh immigrants came to North America around 1900, many of them former soldiers in the British Indian Army who found work on railroads, in lumber mills and on farms in California and British Columbia. The first gurdwara in the United States opened in Stockton, California, in 1912. Early Sikh immigrants faced laws that barred Asian immigration and land ownership. In 1923, in United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind, the Supreme Court ruled that a Sikh veteran of the U.S. Army could not become a citizen. Immigration law changed in 1965, and most Sikh Americans today trace their families to the decades since then.

The Chicago area has a substantial Sikh community, with gurdwaras in Palatine, where the Sikh Religious Society built one of the region's largest, and in other suburbs and neighborhoods. Sikh Americans work in every field, from trucking, in which Sikhs make up a noticeable share of drivers, to medicine, engineering and politics. Turbaned Sikhs have sometimes been mistaken for Muslims and attacked, especially after September 11, 2001. In 2012 a gunman killed six worshipers at a gurdwara in Oak Creek, Wisconsin, about eighty miles north of Chicago; a seventh victim died of his wounds in 2020.

Sikh organizations respond to such events with education and, characteristically, with langar. After Oak Creek, the Wisconsin community reopened its kitchen and invited neighbors of every faith to eat. Understanding the difference between a Sikh turban and Muslim dress, and knowing why a Sikh might carry a kirpan, is part of the practical purpose of a course like this one. The goal is to read the signs around you accurately, so that fear built on confusion has less room to grow.

words.d: a community living outside its homeland; most Sikhs live in Punjab, but millions live in a worldwide diaspora
the first Sikh house of worship in the United States, opened in California in 1912
a Sikh U.S. Army veteran whose 1923 Supreme Court case denied citizenship to immigrants from India

lessons.title: Mahavira, the Conqueror
lessons.mainIdea: Jains follow the teaching of Mahavira, the last of twenty-four Tirthankaras, who taught a path of self-conquest and non-harm.
reading: In the same century and the same region of northeastern India where tradition places the Buddha, another teacher left home to seek liberation. Jains call him *Mahavira*, Great Hero. His given name was Vardhamana, and tradition says he was born to a ruling family near the city of Vaishali, in what is now the Indian state of Bihar. Traditional Jain dates place his life at 599 to 527 BCE; many historians put him somewhat later, in the fifth century BCE. Jains do not regard him as the founder of their tradition but as its most recent great teacher.

According to Jain tradition, Mahavira was the twenty-fourth *Tirthankara*, a word meaning ford-maker, one who builds a crossing over the river of birth and death so others can follow. The twenty-third, Parshvanatha, is placed by tradition about 250 years earlier, and most historians accept that he was a real teacher. Jains hold that the tradition itself is eternal and that Tirthankaras appear in every age to restore it. This is why a Jain would object to the sentence Jainism was founded by Mahavira.

Tradition says that at age thirty Mahavira gave up his home, his wealth and eventually his clothing and spent about twelve years wandering, fasting and meditating, often enduring abuse without responding. At the end of that time Jains believe he attained *kevala jnana*, complete knowledge, becoming a *Jina*, a conqueror. The word Jain means a follower of the Jina. What Mahavira conquered, in Jain understanding, was not an enemy but his own attachments and passions. He taught for about thirty years and organized a community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen, and Jains note that nuns outnumbered monks from the beginning.

Jains believe Mahavira died at Pavapuri, in Bihar, and attained final liberation. The Buddhist scriptures mention him under the name Nigantha Nataputta as a rival teacher, which gives historians an outside witness to his existence. His teaching survives in scriptures called the *Agamas*, written in an ancient language called Ardhamagadhi, though Jains disagree about which texts are authentic, as a later lesson explains.

words.d: Great Hero; the title of Vardhamana, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara, whose teaching Jains follow
a ford-maker; one of twenty-four great teachers who, Jains believe, show the way across the river of rebirth
a conqueror of one's own passions and attachments; Jains are followers of the Jina

the Jain scriptures preserving Mahavira's teaching, in the ancient Ardhamagadhi language

lessons.title: Ahimsa and the Five Vows
lessons.mainIdea: Jain life is organized around ahimsa, non-harm toward every living being, expressed in five vows kept strictly by monastics and more moderately by laypeople.
reading: A Jain monk in western India walks slowly along a road at dawn, sweeping the ground ahead of him with a soft brush of wool before each step. He wears a cloth over his mouth. He will not eat after sunset, and he will not eat root vegetables at all. Each of these habits follows from one principle: *ahimsa*, non-harm. The brush moves insects out of his path. The cloth keeps him from swallowing tiny creatures. Cooking after dark might burn insects drawn to the flame. Pulling up a root kills the whole plant and the small lives in the soil around it.

Jains take ahimsa further than any other major tradition because of how they understand life. According to Jain teaching, every living being has a *jiva*, a soul, and souls dwell not only in animals but in plants, and in the tiniest single-sensed beings of earth, water, fire and air. Harm to any of them attaches karma to the soul, as the next lesson explains. A Jain scripture, the Acharanga Sutra, teaches that no living creature should be killed, treated with violence, abused, tormented or driven away, and calls this the pure and eternal law taught by those who know.

The first of the five Jain vows is ahimsa. The other four are *satya*, truthfulness; *asteya*, not taking what is not given; *brahmacharya*, chastity; and *aparigraha*, non-possession or non-attachment. Monks and nuns take these as the *mahavratas*, the great vows, in their full form: they own almost nothing, do not travel by vehicle, and depend on food offered by laypeople. Laypeople take the same five as *anuvratas*, lesser vows, adapted to family and working life: a strict vegetarian diet, honesty in business, faithfulness in marriage, and limits on what they accumulate.

Jains are divided into two main branches that agree on these vows but differ in practice. *Digambara* monks, whose name means sky-clad, wear no clothing as the fullest expression of non-possession, and this branch holds that women must be reborn as men before final liberation. *Svetambara* monks and nuns, white-clad, wear simple white robes, and this branch holds that women can reach liberation and that the nineteenth Tirthankara was a woman. The two branches also disagree about which scriptures are authentic. Both are ancient, and both are active today.

words.d: non-harm; the first Jain vow, extended to every living being, including the smallest
a soul; Jains believe every living being, down to single-sensed beings of earth, water, fire and air, has one
non-possession or non-attachment; the fifth Jain vow
the five great vows taken in full by Jain monks and nuns; laypeople take the same five as lesser vows
the sky-clad branch of Jainism, whose monks wear no clothing
the white-clad branch of Jainism, whose monks and nuns wear simple white robes

lessons.title: Karma as Matter, and Many Viewpoints
lessons.mainIdea: Jains understand karma as fine matter that clings to the soul, and they teach that no single viewpoint captures the whole truth.
reading: Hindus, Buddhists and Sikhs all use the word karma, but Jains mean something unusually specific by it. In Jain teaching, *karma* is a kind of extremely fine physical matter that fills the universe. Every action driven by passion, especially anger, pride, deceit and greed, draws karmic particles to the soul, where they stick like dust to a wet cloth. The karma clouds the soul's natural qualities, which Jains describe as infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy, and it determines the soul's next birth.

The Jain path is therefore a two-part program. First, stop new karma from coming in, which Jains call *samvara*; the five vows do this by removing the passions that attract it. Second, burn off the karma already there, which Jains call *nirjara*; fasting, meditation and patient endurance of hardship do this. When all karma is gone, Jains believe the soul rises to the top of the universe. There it dwells forever in perfect knowledge and bliss as a *siddha*, a liberated being. Jains do not believe in a creator God. The universe, in Jain teaching, has always existed. The Tirthankaras and siddhas are revered as examples, not as gods who grant favors.

One consequence of this teaching is a strong emphasis on individual effort. Where Sikhs speak of the Guru's grace, and Christians of God's grace, Jains hold that no one else can remove your karma for you. Jain temples are full of images of Tirthankaras seated in meditation, and worshipers offer rice, flowers and lamps before them, but Jain teachers explain that the Tirthankara does not respond; the worship shapes the worshiper. The annual festival of Paryushana, lasting eight or ten days, ends with each Jain asking forgiveness from everyone they may have harmed, with the words micchami dukkadam, may my wrongdoing be forgiven.

Jain philosophy is also known for *anekantavada*, the doctrine of many-sidedness: reality is complex, and any single statement about it captures only part of the truth. Jain teachers illustrate this with the story of blind men describing an elephant, each touching one part and each partly right. From this follows a habit of saying in some respect before a claim. Modern Jains often present anekantavada as intellectual ahimsa, non-violence toward other viewpoints. It is a useful idea for a course that asks students to compare traditions without ranking them.

words.d: in Jain teaching, fine matter drawn to the soul by passionate action, which clouds the soul and shapes its rebirth

wearing away karma already attached to the soul, through fasting, meditation and endurance

lessons.title: Jains Today and Gandhi's Debt
lessons.mainIdea: Jains are a small community with wide influence, including on Gandhi's practice of non-violence and on a Chicago suburb's temple.
reading: Jains number about four to five million people, by common estimates, the great majority in India, especially in the western states of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. That is less than half of one percent of India's population. Yet Jains have an outsized presence in Indian business, banking, publishing and philanthropy. The vows steered them away from farming and soldiering and toward trade. Jain communities have long funded hospitals, animal shelters and schools. Jain temples such as those at Mount Abu in Rajasthan and Palitana in Gujarat are among the most intricately carved buildings in India.

Jainism's best-known influence on world history runs through Mohandas Gandhi. Gandhi was born in 1869 in Gujarat, in a Hindu family. Jains were numerous in his region, his mother kept frequent religious fasts, and before he sailed to London in 1888 a Jain monk administered the vows she asked him to take. As a young lawyer, Gandhi corresponded with a Jain poet and jeweler named Shrimad Rajchandra. He later named Rajchandra as one of the three people who most influenced his thinking. Gandhi's insistence on ahimsa as an active force, his fasts, and his refusal to call his opponents wholly wrong all show the marks of this exposure. Gandhi drew on many sources, though, and remained a Hindu.

Jainism came to Chicago's attention in 1893. That year a young Jain lawyer named Virchand Gandhi, no relation to Mohandas, spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions, the first major interfaith gathering in the United States. Today the Jain Society of Metropolitan Chicago maintains a temple in Bartlett, a western suburb, with white marble carving in the traditional style. Jain communities exist in most large American cities. Estimates of Jains in the United States range from about 100,000 to 200,000.

Modern Jain practice includes questions that outsiders often find striking. Some Jains, usually elderly or terminally ill, choose *sallekhana*, a fast to the death undertaken with a teacher's permission as the final act of non-attachment; Indian courts have debated whether it should be protected as religious practice. Jain communities also run animal shelters called panjrapoles, some of them centuries old, and bird hospitals, and have been early voices in vegetarian and environmental movements. Each of these follows from the same conviction the monk with the brush was living out: that every life counts, down to the smallest.

a Jain poet and jeweler whose letters Gandhi credited as a major influence on his thought
